title: Testing — TestBed, Vitest (v21+), component harnesses, mocking
exp: Angular testing is tested less often in product company interviews but is a common question at companies that prioritize quality. Know TestBed setup, how to test OnPush components, how to mock services, and the Vitest setup (Angular 21+). Signal-based testing patterns are now relevant.
pts: **`TestBed.configureTestingModule`:** sets up an Angular testing environment; declare the component under test and its dependencies (real or mocked)
**`ComponentFixture<T>`:** wrapper around the component; `.componentInstance` (component class), `.nativeElement` (DOM), `.detectChanges()` (trigger CD)
**Testing OnPush:** must call `fixture.detectChanges()` after every state change — OnPush doesn't auto-detect outside the test context
**Mock services:** `jasmine.createSpyObj('UserService', ['getUser'])` or a plain object with jest/vitest `vi.fn()` methods
**`HttpClientTestingModule` / `provideHttpClientTesting()`:** provides a test implementation of HttpClient; use `HttpTestingController.expectOne(url)` to intercept and respond
**Component harnesses (CDK):** `HarnessLoader.getHarness(MatButtonHarness)` — interact with Material components in tests through a stable API instead of fragile DOM selectors
**Testing signals:** signals work synchronously in tests — `component.count.set(5); fixture.detectChanges(); expect(el.textContent).toBe('5')`
**Vitest (Angular 21+, default):** replaces Karma; faster, runs in Node.js; configure via `vitest.config.ts`; uses `describe`, `it`, `expect` like Jest
**`fakeAsync` + `tick(n)`:** fake time to test debounced or delayed operations without real waiting
pr: Write a TestBed test for a component that uses a signal and makes an HTTP call

viz.note: Setup pattern: configureTestingModule → createComponent → detectChanges (init) → [act] → detectChanges (update) → assert

qa.q: What is the difference between shallow and deep component testing in Angular?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Shallow testing (using NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA or stub children): only the component under test is fully rendered; child components are replaced with empty stubs. Faster and more isolated but doesn't verify integration with children. Deep testing (declaring all child components): renders the full component tree. More realistic but slower and more fragile. For unit tests, shallow is preferred; for integration tests that verify component composition, deep is appropriate. The Angular CDK HarnessLoader provides a middle ground for testing specific child component interactions.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: Why do you need to call fixture.detectChanges() in Angular tests?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Angular does not run change detection automatically in the test environment. fixture.detectChanges() triggers one round of change detection: it initialises the component (ngOnInit runs on the first call), then updates the DOM to reflect the current component state. For OnPush components, you MUST call detectChanges() after every state change or the template won't update. Always call it: once in beforeEach after creating the component (initial render), and once after every state change in test cases.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

qa.q: What is the Angular CDK component harness and why use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CDK component harnesses provide a stable API for testing components — especially Angular Material components. Instead of querying the DOM directly (fixture.nativeElement.querySelector('.mat-button')), which breaks when Material changes its DOM structure, you use HarnessLoader.getHarness(MatButtonHarness) and call harness.click(). Benefits: tests are decoupled from implementation details, work consistently across browsers, and don't break on Material version upgrades. You can also write custom harnesses for your own components.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: How does Vitest differ from Karma for Angular tests?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Karma launches a real browser (Chrome/Firefox), runs tests inside it, and reports results back — slow startup, requires a display. Vitest runs in Node.js using jsdom for DOM simulation — starts in milliseconds, runs tests in parallel, and integrates with the Vite build pipeline. Vitest is up to 10x faster for unit tests. Angular 21 made Vitest the default test runner for new projects. The test syntax is nearly identical (describe/it/expect) — the main migration work is configuration and replacing Karma-specific setup.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: How do you test a component that uses signals?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Signals are synchronous — reading and setting them is immediate, unlike Observables. To test: set the signal value with component.mySignal.set(value); call fixture.detectChanges(); then assert on the DOM. For computed signals: set the source signals, call detectChanges, assert the computed result. For effects: effects run during change detection, so fixture.detectChanges() is enough to trigger them. Signal-based tests are generally simpler than Observable-based tests because there's no async, no tick, no subscribe needed for state changes.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular Signals maintain an internal reactive dependency graph (ReactiveNode). When a signal value updates, it marks dependent computed nodes as stale without running change detection immediately. Evaluation happens lazily when read, updating only impacted DOM bindings.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Writing to signals inside an effect() can trigger infinite reactive loops or untracked state dependencies. Fix: use computed() or linkedSignal() for derived state sync, keeping effect() strictly for un-tracked side effects like logging or localStorage.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide fine-grained, synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require learning new primitives (input(), output(), model()) compared to classic RxJS BehaviorSubjects.
